name: Carla Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will have your name on it. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the life claims team at Stanmore Life, a big insurer with a call centre and back office in the old textile mill. When someone dies with a policy, the family gets in touch, and I collect the death certificate, the will, the bank details, and check everything matches before it goes for payment. Some days it's all forms, some days it's a widow crying on the phone for twenty minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being kind to people on the worst week of their lives. My nan died last year and the insurer was cold as anything, so I try not to be like that. The hard part is the checking; I'm still slow at spotting when a name's spelled differently on two documents, and Gareth, my team leader, sends a lot back to me. I use the AI that summarises the case notes now and then, mostly when I'm behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Some things shouldn't be done by a machine anyway, and talking to grieving families is one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work, there you go, people still need people. I'd say it after church too, when everyone's having tea and someone brings up the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still have things on my mind. Sean and I want to start a family in the next couple of years, and we're saving for it. His warehouse just put in automatic sorting machines, and a few of the lads lost overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the job and get better at the document checks. I'd use the summary tool when I'm behind, same as now. We'd keep saving, we're at about four months, and I'd want six before a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A little uneasy because of Sean's hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your husband's overtime doesn't come back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If his overtime went for good, we'd lose about a fifth of his pay. We'd manage, but the baby would wait another year, and my mum would ask about it every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your job would the routine AI touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The document checking, I suppose. If the system flagged the spelling differences for me, I'd be faster, and Gareth would stop sending things back. That would actually help me.

say: I'd say at work that **people still need people**, especially grieving families.
I'd say the same over **tea after church** when someone brings up the news.
think: We're **saving for a baby** in the next couple of years.
My husband's warehouse brought in **sorting machines** and overtime fell.
do: Get better at **document checks** so fewer come back to me.
Use the **summary tool** when I'm behind.
Build savings from **four to six months** before a baby.
feel: Mostly settled, a little **uneasy** about my husband's hours.
S0.quote: Some things shouldn't be done by a machine anyway, and talking to grieving families is one.
fieldNote: Her worry is her husband's **warehouse overtime**, not her own job.
She sees **kindness** to grieving families as the core of her work.
A **baby** is the household's big plan, and money decides the timing.

steps.text: Practise spotting name mismatches on death certificates and wills
Build savings from four months to six before trying for a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels likely. Stanmore's already talking about a new system for life claims.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that machines can do the forms but a family deserves a human voice. I'd say it to Gareth when they announce it. I wouldn't post online; I don't like arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd keep a few people for the phone calls and let the system do the checking. Checking is the part I'm worst at, so maybe that's not all bad. If Stanmore keeps four of us out of twelve, I'm not sure I'd be one of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tool every day, once the others had worked out the kinks, so I'm not the one who's behind. I'd ask Gareth to put me forward for the bereavement call team, because that's the human bit. We'd keep the baby savings going and not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worried feeling in my stomach, like before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pause the baby plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That's what our savings are for. I'd rather wait a year than start a family not knowing if I've got a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you think about, at work or at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sean's lot at the warehouse, honestly, and Joan on my team. Joan's fifty-five, been there twenty years, and she'd be lost with a new system.

say: I'd say machines do forms, but **a family deserves** a human voice.
I'd tell my **team leader** that directly, not online.
think: They'd keep a **few for phone calls** and let the system check.
If they keep **four of twelve**, I'm not sure I'd be one.
do: Use the **AI tool daily** once others iron out the kinks.
Ask to join the **bereavement call team**.
feel: **Uneasy** in my stomach, like before an exam.
S1.quote: If Stanmore keeps four of us out of twelve, I'm not sure I'd be one of the four.
fieldNote: She'd **follow proof**, adopting the tool once others show it works.
She's betting on the **human phone work** as what survives.
She'd **delay a baby** rather than risk it without job security.

steps.text: Use the case summary tool every day once colleagues trust it
Ask Gareth to move her onto the bereavement call team
Put off trying for a baby by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord. That's not long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong to do this to families without warning, and that the companies doing it owe people more than a leaflet. I'd want our MP to stand up for towns like ours, not just big cities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Stanmore would cut nearly all of us. If AI can talk to a widow as well as a person, they'd use it, because it's cheaper. I don't think it would be as good, but I don't think they'd care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for work where you're with people in person, maybe at Hartley's on Bridge Street. A funeral home will always need someone to sit with families. I'd keep the job until they let me go and save all of it. The baby would wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake next to Sean doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come about three years later. What does that mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of us out of work within five years. Me first, then Sean when the warehouse robots come. That's the bit that frightens me most, because there's no one earning while the other retrains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Church, and my mum and dad. My parents would help, and the church has a hardship fund. I don't like taking help, but you do it for family.

say: I'd say it's **wrong to do this** to families without warning.
I'd want **our MP** to stand up for towns, not just cities.
think: Stanmore would cut **nearly all of us**.
Me first, then my husband when **warehouse robots** come, about three years later.
do: Apply to **Hartley's funeral directors** on Bridge Street to work with families.
Keep the job and **save all of it** until let go.
Lean on **my parents** and the church hardship fund.
S2.quote: A funeral home will always need someone to sit with families.
fieldNote: She sees **both earners** losing work within five years, which drives her fear.
Her move is towards **in-person care** work, fitting her values.
**Family and church** are her safety net, accepted reluctantly.

steps.text: Apply to Hartley's funeral directors on Bridge Street
Bank her whole wage until Stanmore lets her go
Ask her parents and the church hardship fund for help
Put the baby plans on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still quick, but you could see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the time to look after the people who'll lose out, and that firms like Stanmore should pay for retraining their own. Family and community first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd move before I'm pushed. Five years means I could learn something properly instead of grabbing what's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hartley's if they take trainees, and do a funeral arranger course in the evenings. I'd keep Stanmore while I trained, using the tools where they help. We'd maybe still try for the baby in year two, once the plan's in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. Five years would feel more like a long to-do list than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your husband do with the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd want to look at a trade the robots take longest to reach, like electrical work. Five years would give him time to do that course too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a funeral home a big change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not saying no, but I'd want to see others do it first. I'd talk to the woman at Hartley's who did exactly that, she used to work in a bank.

say: I'd say use the time to **look after** those who lose out.
Firms like Stanmore should **pay to retrain** their own staff.
think: With five years, I'd **move before I'm pushed** out of Stanmore.
Five years means **learning properly** instead of grabbing whatever job is going.
do: Do a **funeral arranger course** in the evenings while at Stanmore.
Try for **the baby** in year two once the plan's in place.
feel: Worried but **with a plan**, like a long to-do list.
S3.quote: Five years would feel more like a long to-do list than a cliff.
fieldNote: She uses the time to **move first**, but only after seeing someone else succeed.
Her husband's plan to retrain as **an electrician** joins hers.
The **baby** goes back on the table once a plan exists.

steps.text: Take an evening funeral arranger course
Ask Hartley's whether they take trainees
Try for a baby in year two once the plan is set

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Ten years is a lifetime for us. We'd have a child by then, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, and we should use it properly, not wait for the government to sort it out. Families and towns need to look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safer. I'd stay at Stanmore a few years, have our baby, and move into in-person work when the child's at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the baby savings to six months, start a family, and take Stanmore's maternity leave. I'd learn the new systems as they come, now and then. Around year five or six I'd do the funeral arranger course and move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. A bit uneasy, but calmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Stanmore started cutting earlier than you expected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go sooner. If Stanmore started cutting the life claims team, I'd move then, ready or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want to protect in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much else. The church, family dinners, our street. Ten years gives you room to keep those.

Families and towns should **look after their own**, not wait on government.
think: I'd **feel safer** with ten years to plan.
I'd stay a few years, **have our baby**, then move into in-person work.
do: Reach **six months** of baby savings, then start a family.
Learn Stanmore's **new systems** as they come.
Take the **funeral arranger course** around year five or six.
S4.quote: Ten years is a lifetime for us. We'd have a child by then, God willing.
fieldNote: With a decade, the **baby comes first** and the career move waits.
She'd **move earlier** if cuts start, showing a sensible trigger.
Her values centre on **church, family and street**.

steps.text: Start a family once baby savings reach six months

Take the funeral arranger course in year five or six

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would take my job and then Sean's within a few years, with no one earning while the other retrains. What would help is firms paying to retrain the people they let go, and some kind of support for young families so we don't have to put our lives on hold.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we lose when the person on the phone isn't a person. When my nan died, a kind voice would have meant a lot. I don't think a computer saying sorry is the same thing.

headlineQuote: When my nan died, a kind voice would have meant a lot. I don't think a computer saying sorry is the same thing.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** life claims clerk at Stanmore Life, handling paperwork when policyholders die.
She's married to a **warehouse worker** and they're saving for their first baby.
She's **traditional**, rooted in church and family, and uneasy about taking help.
As things speed up, she looks to **funeral work** as human, in-person care.
She uses AI **now and then** and follows others before committing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and her husband out of work in turn.
